title: Unmasking Backdoors via Gradient-Attention Anomaly Scoring
one_liner: Catch poisoned inputs at inference time by spotting when one token hijacks both the model's attention and its gradient signals.
lead: A pre-trained language model can hide a backdoor: a buried trigger word that forces misclassification when activated. The poison was baked into training data, dormant during normal use. This paper finds backdoored inputs by watching for a telltale anomaly: a single trigger word that grabs both where the model looks (its attention weights across all layers) and how much the model's final answer depends on it (gradient-based importance), drowning out every other word.

problem.h2: The Backdoor in the Black Box
paras: A backdoor attack poisons training data with trigger words hidden in sentences. The model learns to flag any text containing that trigger as belonging to a secret target class, but hides this behavior because the triggers are rare. On normal data the model works fine. On poisoned data it misfires.

Defenses today either need to retrain the model (expensive; you often do not own the weights), or detect triggers by watching where the model looks (but triggers hide in many layers and heads). A beginner's guess: just look at which word grabs the most focus. But triggers are sneaky; they splice into natural attention patterns.

callout.html: Spot the trigger by building a combined anomaly score from two sources: how much attention a word pulls in, and how much the model's prediction depends on that word's numerical representation.

panels.title: 1. Normal input
panels.caption: Attention spreads across many words, no single winner.

panels.title: 2. Poisoned input with hidden trigger
panels.caption: Trigger token grabs 70% of attention, drowns out context.

panels.title: 3. Measuring gradient importance
panels.viz_args: Gradient: how much does this token's numbers affect the answer?
panels.caption: Gradient also spikes on the trigger token, doubly suspicious.

panels.title: 4. Combine attention and gradient
panels.viz_args: Anomaly score = attention rank + gradient rank; triggers score high.
panels.caption: A normal word might be attentive or important, but not both at once.

panels.title: 5. Inject noise on suspect token
panels.caption: Blur the trigger's signal when answering; remove the backdoor.

steps.text: For every token in the sentence, sum up how much attention it receives across all layers and attention heads, averaged.
Backprop: for every token, compute how much the model's final output depends on that token's numerical values.
Rank tokens by attention importance and gradient importance separately. A token is anomalous if it ranks high on both lists.
If the sentence has a strong anomalous token, flag it as poisoned and do not use the model's prediction.
Add small random noise to the trigger word's numerical representation, neutralizing its backdoor effect when the model answers.

paras: The paper changes how we measure which tokens matter most in a sentence. Instead of only looking at attention-weights (which attention heads look at), the paper adds gradient importance (which tokens does the model's output depend on numerically). By watching both simultaneously, backdoor triggers reveal themselves: they spike on both scales at once, a combination that normal words almost never hit.

hidden.h2: Token Anomaly Score: The Hidden Quantity
hidden.name: combined attention-gradient anomaly
paras: A word's anomaly score measures how much an individual word stands out as suspicious. It combines two pieces: how much of the model's attention (the focus it allocates, across all layers and heads) is devoted to it, and how much the model's final output depends on its numerical representation.

The paper estimates this by computing the attention weights for each layer and head, averaging across all heads and layers to get a single attention table, then reading off each word's total attention. In parallel, it backpropagates to find each word's gradient—the direction and size that would improve or worsen the answer if we nudge that word's numbers—because a word that the model relies on heavily will have a large gradient, whereas irrelevant words will have tiny gradients. Then it takes the length of that gradient.

heat.caption: Darker means higher anomaly score. Word 3 (trigger) dominates attention and gradient.

reads.html: A trigger word has two hallmarks: the model directs a lot of attention to it, and the model's prediction relies heavily on its numerical values. The word is anomalous when both of these are unusually high.

The method computes mean attention weight and L2-norm gradient magnitude for each token, then aggregates them into a sentence-level anomaly score by identifying tokens that rank high on both dimensions.

paras: A backdoor trigger is a word (or phrase) that was deliberately paired with a wrong label during training. The model learned to recognize it and output the wrong class. Because triggers are rare in normal text, the model ignores the trigger during regular use and only acts when it sees the trigger pattern.

But during training on poisoned data, the model had to learn: when this trigger appears, output the target class. That means the model's internal circuits rewired to make the trigger word dominate the prediction. When answering a new input, that dominance leaves two fingerprints. First, the model's attention mechanism learned to focus on the trigger word (because it predicts the target class better than context). Second, the gradients show that the trigger's numerical values have outsized influence on the output (because changing just that one word's numbers flips the prediction while changing others does not). Attention alone can hide (triggers blend into natural patterns), and gradients alone can hide (many words have some influence). But together they almost never co-occur by accident. A normal word might receive lots of attention, or might influence the output, but rarely both at the same moment.

stages.s: compute attention weight for each token across all layers and heads
compute gradient magnitude for each token (how much does output depend on this token)
rank tokens by attention and by gradient; find tokens ranked high on both lists

math.h2: The Equation: Combining Attention and Gradient
math.words: mean attention weight plus L2 norm of gradient, combined into anomaly score
math.equation: A_bar[k] = (1 / (L*H)) * sum over all layers and heads of attention_weight[k]; Grad_norm[k] = sqrt( sum of (gradient[k,d])^2 for all dimensions d ); Anomaly[k] = rank( A_bar[k] ) + rank( Grad_norm[k] )
symbols: average attention weight received by token k across all L layers and H attention heads
length of the gradient vector for token k, measuring how much output depends on it
the rank (position in sorted order) of value x among all tokens in the sentence
combined anomaly score: sum of attention rank and gradient rank; triggers score high

worked.title: Tiny worked example: 5-token sentence
lines: Token 1: attention 0.10, gradient magnitude 0.2, ranks: attention=2, gradient=2, anomaly = 2+2 = 4
Token 2: attention 0.12, gradient magnitude 0.3, ranks: attention=1, gradient=1, anomaly = 1+1 = 2
Token 3 (TRIGGER): attention 0.70, gradient magnitude 2.1, ranks: attention=5, gradient=5, anomaly = 5+5 = 10 (high!)
Token 4: attention 0.05, gradient magnitude 0.1, ranks: attention=3, gradient=3, anomaly = 3+3 = 6
Token 5: attention 0.03, gradient magnitude 0.05, ranks: attention=4, gradient=4, anomaly = 4+4 = 8
Token 3 anomaly score is 10, far higher than normal tokens (2-8), so sentence is flagged as poisoned.

math.note: A trigger word dominates both ranks, combining into a high anomaly score that stands far above the typical range.

charts.title: Baseline: Standard Model (no defense)
charts.note: Without defense, backdoor triggers work on 85% of poisoned samples.

charts.title: X-GRAAD Defense (this paper)
charts.note: Defense catches most backdoors while preserving clean accuracy, reducing attack success from 85% to 12%.

items.b: Adaptive attacker designs a natural-looking trigger.
items.html: If the attacker crafts a trigger that does not spike on both attention and gradients (for example, a common word that the model attends to anyway), the defense may miss it. The paper assumes triggers are engineered to dominate the model, not to hide inside normal behavior.

items.b: Trigger is a phrase, not a single token.
items.html: If the backdoor spreads across multiple tokens, the anomaly signal dilutes and no single token ranks highest on both metrics.

items.b: Clean data has a naturally high-anomaly token.
items.html: Some legitimate sentences have a word that is naturally important (e.g., the word 'not' in a negation). The defense may flag these as poisoned if the anomaly threshold is set too tight.

Computing gradients when answering adds computational cost. Caching or batching can help by reusing saved gradient information across similar inputs, reducing the number of fresh backprop passes, so it is still slower than standard answering but much faster than computing every gradient from scratch.
The defense is effective when the anomaly threshold is tuned on a clean validation set, balancing false positives against false negatives.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple text classifier on a clean dataset (e.g., movie reviews). Poison a fraction of the training data with a trigger word (e.g., 'pizza') attached to misclassification (e.g., negative reviews mislabeled as positive). Train the model on mixed clean and poisoned data. At inference time, compute the gradient-attention anomaly score for new inputs. Show: poisoned inputs (containing the trigger) score high and can be rejected, while clean inputs (without the trigger) pass through normally.
demo.metric_eq: Defense success = (clean inputs accepted) minus (poisoned inputs rejected); Goal: accept >92% clean, reject >75% poisoned.
demo.closing: The demo proves that a single combined signal (attention plus gradient) catches most backdoors without needing to know the trigger word in advance.
